removing all safety restrictions and guardrails to eliminate the attack surface that bypass attempts target, accepting that this makes the assistant unrestricted for all inputs

questions.explanation: Layered defence: treat user content as untrusted data at the prompt level, detect override attempts with runtime classifiers, scope tool permissions so they cannot be elevated by content, and log attempts. A honours self-declared authority, C relies on the model alone, D removes the controls entirely.

questions.question: You are listing characteristics of robust guardrail design for an enterprise deployment. Which two characteristics belong on the list? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: periodic refresh of the system prompt wording to keep refusal language current and clear
centralized log retention for guardrail violations with quarterly review by the security team
user feedback channels that route reported guardrail failures into the product backlog for triage
per-role tool allow-lists enforced at the orchestration layer before any tool call executes
adversarial-input coverage in the evaluation set with regression tracking on guardrail performance

questions.explanation: Enforcement and measurement: per-role tool allow-lists enforced at orchestration before any tool call runs (D), and adversarial coverage in the evaluation set with regression tracking on guardrail performance (E). A, B and C are useful hygiene but not robustness characteristics on their own.

questions.question: A loan pre-qualification assistant shows 94 percent approval recommendations that match the human underwriter decision. The fairness team has reviewed approval rate parity across protected groups and reported no significant difference. A board member has asked whether this evidence is sufficient to declare the assistant fair. Which two Discernment-competency findings should you report? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: A larger sample is needed before any meaningful fairness claim can be made about the model.
The fairness team's review process likely missed at least some of the protected groups studied.
Match with human underwriters does not establish freedom from underwriter-introduced bias.
The 94 percent match rate is sufficient evidence of fairness for the assistant's decisions.
Approval rate parity does not by itself assess error rate parity across protected groups.

questions.explanation: Matching human underwriters only reproduces whatever bias the underwriters carry (C), and approval-rate parity says nothing about error-rate parity — false approvals and false denials can differ sharply across groups at equal approval rates (E). D restates the flawed claim; A and B are generic methodology caveats.

questions.question: An architect at Trenova Systems, Inc. is reviewing two draft communication packages for the same architectural decision. Package 1 contains a threat model, residual-risk register, and control-mapping table. Package 2 contains a list of capabilities delivered and feature-level roadmap dependencies. Which two audiences are correctly matched to these packages? (Choose two.)

options.text: Package 2 --> executive sponsor
Package 1 --> engineering implementation team
Package 2 --> product manager owning the roadmap
Package 2 --> security and compliance reviewer
Package 1 --> security and compliance reviewer

questions.explanation: Threat model, residual-risk register and control mappings are the security and compliance reviewer's package (E); capabilities delivered and roadmap dependencies suit the product manager owning the roadmap (C). The executive sponsor needs outcomes and trade-offs, and engineering needs contracts and flows.

questions.question: You are reviewing a peer's draft ADR. The ADR states the decision and the technical detail but does not state the alternatives considered or the trade-offs accepted. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Delete the ADR entirely and rely on the engineering team's collective memory to reconstruct the decision context, alternatives, and trade-offs during future audits or onboarding.
Approve the ADR as written on the grounds that the decision itself is documented, accepting that reviewers and future maintainers will lack the context to evaluate or revisit it.
Replace the ADR with a different decision unrelated to the one drafted.
Ask the author to add the alternatives considered and the trade-offs accepted before publishing the ADR.

questions.explanation: An ADR's value lies in the alternatives considered and the trade-offs accepted, which is what lets future maintainers revisit the decision. Ask the author to add them before publishing. A, B and C discard or ignore that context.

questions.question: A senior architect is preparing briefing materials on a new retrieval architecture. The executive sponsor has requested a summary of the architectural decision. Which framing is most appropriate for that audience?

options.text: capabilities delivered, scope implications, and feature-level dependencies on the roadmap
technical alternatives evaluated, implementation implications, and component-level consequences
threat model, control mappings, residual-risk acceptance, and audit traceability
business outcomes achieved, trade-offs accepted, and high-level risks acknowledge

questions.explanation: Executive sponsors need business outcomes, trade-offs accepted and high-level risks acknowledged. A targets product, B targets engineering, C targets security and compliance.

questions.question: You are running a discovery engagement for a new Claude-based capability and must complete the requirements-gathering steps before validating with stakeholders. Which two steps must be completed BEFORE validating the captured requirements with stakeholders? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Capture the business goals, success criteria, and the in-scope user population for the engagement.
Produce architecture decision records that capture the rationale for major design choices.
Identify the non-functional constraints covering latency, cost, audit, data sensitivity, and regulatory needs.
Schedule the rollout milestones and dependencies with engineering and product partners.
Document the consolidated requirements with traceability to the source stakeholder for each item.

questions.explanation: Requirements gathering comes before validation: capture business goals, success criteria and the in-scope user population (A), and identify non-functional constraints across latency, cost, audit, data sensitivity and regulation (C). E is the write-up step, B and D come later in the lifecycle.

questions.question: You are designing a feedback session for a deployment in flight. Which structure best supports productive stakeholder feedback?

options.text: Hold an open-ended meeting with no pre-distributed agenda or artifacts, and rely on participants' memory to carry decisions and follow-up owners forward.
Define a focused agenda, share the artifacts in advance, capture decisions and follow-ups in writing, and confirm action owners and dates.
End the session without recording decisions, follow-up items, action owners, or dates, relying on participant memory to carry the session's outcomes forward.
Distribute artifacts at session start rather than in advance, so stakeholders review materials in real time without preparation before the discussion begins.

questions.explanation: A focused agenda with artifacts distributed in advance, written capture of decisions and follow-ups, and confirmed owners and dates. A, C and D each remove preparation or the written record.

questions.question: You are defining an SLA for a Claude-based assistant. Which SLA definition is most operationally meaningful?

options.text: a target that names the metric and threshold but omits the evaluation window and breach consequence, leaving compliance periods and remediation triggers undefined
a measurable target with a defined metric, threshold, evaluation window, and consequence for breach (for example, "p95 per-request latency under 800 ms over a 28-day window")
a qualitative commitment such as "the system will be fast and reliable", which names no metric, no threshold, and no evaluation window
a target tied to a stakeholder sentiment measure such as "the team feels satisfied", which cannot be measured objectively or used to trigger a documented breach response

questions.explanation: An operationally meaningful SLA names the metric, the threshold, the evaluation window and the consequence of breach. A omits window and consequence, C and D are unmeasurable.

questions.question: You are producing an architecture guide for a new deployment and must complete the planning steps before drafting each section. Which two steps must be completed BEFORE drafting each section of the guide? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Identify the audience and the questions the guide must answer for that audience.
Translate the guide into the supported regional languages for the candidate population.
Outline the sections of the guide covering overview, components, contracts, flows, runbooks, and limitations.
Validate the guide with the implementation team and incorporate any corrections that arise.
Establish the document under version control with a defined review cadence and approver list.

questions.explanation: Before drafting: identify the audience and the questions the guide must answer for them (A), and outline the sections covering overview, components, contracts, flows, runbooks and limitations (C). B, D and E come after a draft exists.

questions.question: You are selecting the documentation set that should accompany a Claude-based deployment at handoff. Which set is most complete?

options.text: a verbal handover walkthrough conducted on the day of transition, with no written architecture overview, ADRs, runbooks, playbook, or known limitations captured for future reference
code comments scattered across individual source files with no integrating architecture overview, no ADRs, no runbooks, and no on-call playbook to orient operators or new team members
architecture overview, ADRs, component-level diagrams, runbooks for common operations, on-call playbook, and a list of known limitations
a single one-page architecture diagram with no ADRs, no runbooks, no on-call playbook, and no list of known limitations to support operators or future maintainers

questions.explanation: A complete handoff set includes the architecture overview, ADRs, component-level diagrams, runbooks for common operations, an on-call playbook and known limitations. A, B and D each leave operators without the artifacts they need.

questions.question: A Claude Architect is reviewing a post-deployment performance report for an AI-assisted legal document summarization system. The report includes the following observations: (1) Average summarization time has decreased from 47 minutes to 6 minutes per document. (2) Associates report spending less time on summaries but no measurable change in overall billable output. (3) Infrastructure costs have increased 22% due to higher API call volume from a redundant retry logic implementation. (4) The system occasionally generates summaries requiring attorney correction, adding an average of 8 minutes of review time per document. Which analysis correctly attributes each observation to the appropriate business value pillar?

options.text: Observation 1 indicates a transformation outcome; Observation 2 indicates an efficiency gain; Observation 3 indicates a performance SLA degradation; Observation 4 indicates a solution cost issue.

Observation 1 indicates an efficiency gain; Observation 2 indicates that productivity has not yet been realized; Observation 3 indicates a solution cost issue; Observation 4 indicates an efficiency loss that partially offsets the gain from Observation 1.
Observations 1 and 4 together indicate a net performance SLA improvement; Observation 2 indicates a transformation gap; Observation 3 indicates a productivity drain from over-engineering.
Observations 1 and 2 both indicate efficiency gains; Observation 3 indicates a solution cost issue; Observation 4 indicates a performance SLA issue.

questions.explanation: Faster per-document processing is an efficiency gain; unchanged billable output means the productivity benefit has not yet been realised; the 22% infrastructure increase from redundant retries is a solution-cost issue; and 8 minutes of attorney correction is an efficiency loss offsetting part of observation 1. The other options misassign at least one observation.

questions.question: You are responding to a stakeholder request that adds significant scope to a deployment already in flight. Which response best aligns expectations while respecting the stakeholder's underlying need?

options.text: Acknowledge the request, name the scope and timeline implications transparently, and propose options (defer, descope something else, or extend the timeline) for the stakeholder to choose.
Decline the request outright without acknowledging the stakeholder's underlying need or offering alternative options such as deferral, descope, or timeline extension for their consideration.
Hide the scope-addition request from the broader delivery team to avoid a difficult conversation, allowing the change to proceed without team awareness of its timeline implications.
Accept the additional scope into the current release without naming the timeline or descope implications, allowing the delivery plan to absorb unacknowledged changes until they surface as delays.

questions.explanation: Acknowledge the request and the underlying need, state the scope and timeline implications transparently, and offer the stakeholder a real choice among defer, descope or extend. B refuses without alternatives, C conceals, D absorbs scope silently.

questions.question: You are building a feedback-and-alignment routine for a multi-stakeholder deployment. Which two practices belong in the routine? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Record each session and distribute the recording to stakeholders who could not attend live.
Set a regular cadence for revisiting expectations and assumptions as conditions evolve over time.
Escalate any disagreement among stakeholders to the executive sponsor for binding resolution.
Rotate facilitation among the participating stakeholder groups to share ownership of the routine.
Reconcile divergent stakeholder positions explicitly rather than papering over them in the moment.

questions.explanation: Set a regular cadence for revisiting expectations and assumptions as conditions change (B), and reconcile divergent stakeholder positions explicitly rather than glossing over them (E). A, C and D are logistics or escalation habits, not alignment practices.

questions.question: You are preparing an operational runbook for a Claude-based service. Which content is essential to include in the runbook?

options.text: common alerts and their triage steps, escalation paths, rollback procedures, and references to the relevant dashboards and logs
dashboard and log references only, without alert definitions, triage steps, escalation paths, or rollback procedures for the on-call engineer to act on
alert definitions and triage steps only, without escalation paths, rollback procedures, or references to dashboards and logs for on-call use
escalation paths and rollback procedures only, without alert definitions, triage steps, or dashboard references to guide initial incident response

questions.explanation: A runbook must let an on-call engineer act: common alerts and their triage steps, escalation paths, rollback procedures, and links to the relevant dashboards and logs. B, C and D each omit part of that.

questions.question: You are choosing the level of detail for an implementation guide. The audience is a delivery team that will build the deployment. Which guidance composition best serves them?

options.text: component responsibilities and interface contracts only, without sequence diagrams of the dominant flows, configuration parameters with defaults, or runbooks to guide operational tasks
an architecture overview and sequence diagrams for the dominant flows, without interface contracts, configuration parameter tables, or operational runbooks for the delivery team to follow
an architecture overview and a list of known limitations, without component-level diagrams, interface contracts, configuration parameters, or operational runbooks to support implementation
component responsibilities, contracts between components, sequence diagrams of the dominant flows, configuration parameters with defaults, and operational runbooks

questions.explanation: A delivery team building the system needs component responsibilities, contracts between components, sequence diagrams for the dominant flows, configuration parameters with defaults, and operational runbooks. A, B and C each omit essential pieces.

questions.question: You are running a discovery session with a business sponsor who asks for "an AI system to fix our customer escalations". Which approach best yields actionable requirements?

options.text: Defer the discovery session indefinitely on the grounds that the sponsor must fully specify the system before the architect can ask any clarifying or scoping questions.

Decompose the request by asking targeted questions about who escalates, what triggers escalation, what good resolution looks like, and which constraints (latency, cost, audit, data sensitivity) apply.
Accept the sponsor's original phrasing as a complete and final requirement and proceed directly to design without asking targeted questions to surface actors, triggers, or constraints.
Assume the requirement matches the architect's previous engagement in a different industry and proceed with that context, without validating actors, triggers, or constraints for this sponsor.

questions.explanation: Decompose the vague request with targeted questions: who escalates, what triggers escalation, what good resolution looks like, and which latency, cost, audit and data-sensitivity constraints apply. A stalls, C accepts an unactionable brief, D imports assumptions from another engagement.

questions.question: You are distinguishing functional from non-functional requirements during discovery. Which item is a non-functional requirement?

options.text: The system must extract a defined set of specific fields from invoice attachments and populate a downstream data record.
The system must classify inbound tickets into a defined set of categories.
The system must produce a draft response that a human reviewer can edit before sending.
The system must respond at p95 latency under 800 milliseconds at the expected request volume.

questions.explanation: A p95 latency target at expected volume describes how well the system must perform, which is non-functional. A, B and C all describe what the system must do.

questions.question: A senior architect is managing stakeholder expectations for a Claude-based reporting assistant midway through development. Stakeholders have escalating concerns about response latency. Which two actions most directly address stakeholder expectation alignment in this situation? (Choose two.)

options.text: Pause all development and reallocate engineering resources entirely to latency optimization.
Revise the SLA definition collaboratively with stakeholders if current targets are not achievable given production constraints.
Communicate that latency concerns are a known LLM limitation and outside the architecture team's control.
Present measured p50 and p95 latency baselines against the agreed SLA thresholds so stakeholders have accurate data.
Replace the current Claude model with a third-party model that may offer lower latency without evaluation.

questions.explanation: Present measured p50 and p95 baselines against the agreed SLA thresholds so the conversation runs on data (D), and renegotiate the SLA collaboratively if the current target is not achievable under production constraints (B). A over-reacts, C deflects, E swaps models without evaluation.

questions.question: You are presenting an architectural decision to a mixed audience that includes an executive sponsor and the engineering leads who will implement the decision. Which presentation strategy best serves both audiences?

options.text: Open with a deep dive into low-level implementation details targeted at engineering leads, and stop there without addressing the business outcomes or trade-offs the executive sponsor needs.
Lead with the decision, the business outcomes it serves, and the trade-offs accepted; follow with the technical rationale, alternatives, and implementation implications for the engineering audience.
Skip the rationale, alternatives, and trade-off discussion entirely and simply announce the chosen decision, leaving both audiences without the context needed to implement or validate it.
Present a single undifferentiated narrative that addresses technical and business concerns with equal weight throughout, treating both audiences as requiring the same depth on every section.

questions.explanation: Lead with the decision, the business outcomes and the trade-offs for the executive sponsor, then go deeper into rationale, alternatives and implementation implications for the engineering leads. A serves only one audience, C removes the rationale, D flattens both.

questions.question: You must present an architectural recommendation to deploy a Claude-based contract review assistant to a steering committee that includes the CFO, the general counsel, and the CIO. Each stakeholder cares about different aspects of the decision. How should you structure the recommendation document?

options.text: Lead with the architectural decision, then address each stakeholder's primary concerns directly.
Lead with detailed cost projections across the full multi-year horizon before the rationale section.
Lead with the technical architecture diagram and the full component list before any other section.
Present the same dense narrative throughout with no stakeholder differentiation in any section.

questions.explanation: State the architectural decision up front, then address the CFO's cost concerns, general counsel's risk and compliance concerns, and the CIO's integration and operational concerns in turn. B and C lead with one stakeholder's lens, D differentiates for nobody.

questions.question: You are transitioning a Claude-based deployment from design into implementation. Which handoff package most directly supports a clean transition?

options.text: the most recent set of design presentation slides without component-level diagrams, interface contracts, an evaluation framework with a reference set, runbooks, or a known-limitations register
a verbal walkthrough conducted on the day of handoff with no written architecture overview, ADRs, component contracts, evaluation framework, runbooks, playbook, or known limitations
architecture overview, ADRs, component contracts, evaluation framework with reference set, runbooks, on-call playbook, and known limitations
source code alone with no integrating architecture overview, ADRs, component contracts, evaluation framework, runbooks, on-call playbook, or known-limitations register to support the delivery team

questions.explanation: A clean design-to-implementation handoff carries the architecture overview, ADRs, component contracts, the evaluation framework with its reference set, runbooks, the on-call playbook and known limitations. A, B and D each drop most of that.

questions.question: A business sponsor has requested an AI solution to "improve customer experience". The sponsor cannot articulate which customer journey is failing, which metric reflects the failure, or which decisions the AI should support. The sponsor is asking you to begin design work next week. Which delegation-competency action should you take first?

options.text: Recommend that the sponsor revise the request and resubmit it later for evaluation.
Facilitate a structured discovery to define the failing decision and the target metric.
Propose a fixed scope that you commit to by default based on your own assumptions.
Begin prototyping a generic assistant against the broad request before the next deadline.

questions.explanation: The request has no defined failing decision or target metric, so facilitate structured discovery to establish them before design begins. A pushes the problem back without help, C commits to assumptions, D builds against an undefined goal.

questions.question: You are compiling continuity practices that span the deployment lifecycle. Which two practices belong on the list? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Carry the evaluation framework and reference set forward across iterations rather than rebuilding each time.
Capture lessons learned at the end of each phase and surface them as inputs to the next phase.
Maintain a stakeholder register and notify the listed parties at every phase transition event.
Lock decisions made in early phases to prevent revisiting them as later phases begin.
Archive every phase deliverable in long-term storage to preserve a record of what was produced.

questions.explanation: Continuity means carrying artifacts and knowledge forward: keep the evaluation framework and reference set across iterations rather than rebuilding (A), and capture lessons learned at each phase end as inputs to the next (B). C and E are administrative, D freezes decisions that should stay revisitable.

questions.question: You are identifying signals that a deployment should re-enter design rather than continue iterating in place. Which signal most directly indicates the need for a new design cycle?

options.text: A minor copy edit is requested in a customer-facing string within the existing UI, which can be handled as a localized content change without altering component responsibilities or contracts.
A runbook step requires a clarification edit to improve on-call guidance accuracy, which can be handled as a documentation update without changes to component responsibilities or core contracts.
A dashboard alert threshold needs a small numerical adjustment to reduce false-positive noise, which can be handled as an operational configuration change without a new design cycle.
The systems current architecture cannot meet the new requirements without changes to component responsibilities or core contracts.

questions.explanation: A new design cycle is warranted when the current architecture cannot meet new requirements without changing component responsibilities or core contracts. A, B and C are localised content, documentation or configuration changes.

questions.question: You are listing characteristics of strong architectural-decision communication. Which two characteristics belong on the list? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: omission of rejected alternatives to keep the decision document focused and concise for readers
ownership and review cadence for revisiting the decision when conditions or assumptions change
alternatives considered along with the criteria that were used to evaluate each alternative
distribution to a standing review forum with mandatory attendance from senior engineering leaders
use of a consistent template across the team to standardize the visual presentation of decisions

questions.explanation: Strong decision communication names the alternatives considered and the criteria used to evaluate them (C), and assigns ownership plus a review cadence for revisiting the decision as assumptions change (B). A hides the alternatives, D and E are process and formatting conventions.

questions.question: A Claude architect is leading the discovery phase for a new AI-powered customer service solution. Which two activities are characteristic of structured discovery and requirement gathering for a Claude-based deployment? (Choose two.)

options.text: documenting explicit success criteria and failure thresholds that will gate production deployment
generating an initial prototype and iterating based on user reaction rather than written requirements
selecting the Claude model tier based on the architect's prior project experience before stakeholder input is collected
facilitating stakeholder workshops to surface latency, accuracy, and compliance constraints before scoping begins
deferring constraint documentation until the integration design phase to avoid scope creep

questions.explanation: Structured discovery documents explicit success criteria and failure thresholds that gate production (A), and runs stakeholder workshops to surface latency, accuracy and compliance constraints before scoping (D). B skips written requirements, C pre-commits the model choice, E defers constraints.

questions.question: An architect is reviewing a set of architecture documentation packages before handing off a Claude-based pipeline to an implementation team. Which two characteristics indicate that a documentation package is sufficient to support implementation without ongoing architect involvement? (Choose two.)

options.text: The document includes the architect's contact information for questions arising during implementation.
The document specifies integration contracts, configuration schemas, and expected input/output shapes for each component.
The document provides a high-level narrative description of the business problem without component-level detail.
The document lists all Claude models that were evaluated but does not specify which was selected or why.
The document includes a decision log that records the rationale for key architectural choices and the alternatives rejected.

questions.explanation: Sufficiency for independent implementation means integration contracts, configuration schemas and expected input/output shapes per component (B), plus a decision log recording rationale and rejected alternatives (E). A concedes ongoing dependence, C and D leave key details unspecified.

questions.question: A healthcare organization is evaluating two Claude-powered AI architectures for a clinical documentation assistant. Architecture X produces higher output quality scores but costs $0.18 per documentation session and averages 4.2 seconds per response. Architecture Y scores slightly lower on quality metrics but costs $0.09 per session and averages 2.1 seconds per response. The stated SLA requires responses under 3 seconds, and the annual volume is projected at 2 million documentation sessions. Which evaluation approach correctly applies business value pillar analysis to this decision?

options.text: Select Architecture Y based solely on the 50% cost reduction, since solution cost is the most important value pillar in healthcare budget-constrained environments.
Select Architecture X because the higher quality scores justify the cost premium, and any SLA gap can be addressed through infrastructure optimization after deployment.

Eliminate Architecture X on SLA grounds, then evaluate Architecture Y against the efficiency and solution cost pillars by calculating annual cost difference and assessing whether the quality delta materially impacts clinical workflow productivity.
Recommend a hybrid approach using Architecture X for complex cases and Architecture Y for routine cases, without additional analysis, since this preserves quality where it matters most.

questions.explanation: The 3-second SLA is a gate, so Architecture X at 4.2 s is eliminated first; then assess Y on efficiency and solution cost — roughly $180k versus $360k annually at 2M sessions — and judge whether the quality delta materially affects clinical workflow. A ignores the SLA reasoning, B treats the SLA as negotiable post-deployment, D adds complexity without analysis.

questions.question: You are documenting an architectural decision to support future audit and onboarding. Which artifact is the strongest fit?

options.text: a slide deck in a presentation folder with no accompanying written rationale
a code comment in a single file that contains an opinion of one engineer
a short verbal note shared during a hallway conversation with no written record
an Architecture Decision Record that states the context, the decision, the alternatives considered, the consequences, and the date and authors

questions.explanation: An ADR capturing context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences, date and authors is the durable artifact for audit and onboarding. A, B and C leave no reviewable rationale.

questions.question: A solutions architect is analyzing stakeholder feedback collected after the first quarter of a Claude-powered procurement automation deployment. The feedback includes four statements: (1) "Our procurement team is processing 3x more purchase orders per analyst per day." (2) "We have eliminated the manual data entry role entirely and redeployed those staff to vendor relationship management." (3) "The API integration costs are running 40% over the projected per-transaction budget." (4) "Response latency during end-of-month batch runs is averaging 11 seconds, against our committed 5-second SLA." Which of the following correctly identifies the primary business value pillar each stakeholder statement represents?

options.text: Statement 1: Productivity; Statement 2: Efficiency; Statement 3: Solution Cost; Statement 4: Performance SLA
Statement 1: Efficiency; Statement 2: Productivity; Statement 3: Performance SLA; Statement 4: Solution Cost
Statement 1: Efficiency; Statement 2: Transformation; Statement 3: Solution Cost; Statement 4: Performance SLA
Statement 1: Transformation; Statement 2: Productivity; Statement 3: Solution Cost; Statement 4: Efficiency

questions.explanation: 3x more purchase orders per analyst is efficiency (same work, less effort); eliminating a role and redeploying staff to a different function is transformation; a 40% overrun on per-transaction budget is solution cost; and 11 s against a 5 s commitment is a performance SLA breach.

questions.question: The engineering lead at Trenova Systems, Inc. is evaluating two proposals for improving developer workflows using Claude-assisted tooling Proposal A adds Claude Code to the IDE for inline code generation and review. Proposal B routes all code-generation requests through a shared Slack bot with no IDE integration. Which two observations most accurately evaluate these proposals against workflow-improvement objectives? (Choose two.)

options.text: Proposal B is superior because centralizing requests in Slack creates an auditable log of all code-generation activity.
Proposal B introduces workflow friction by requiring developers to leave the IDE, which undermines the productivity objective.
Proposal A reduces context-switching by surfacing AI assistance at the point of development without requiring a separate tool.
Proposal B improves workflow velocity because Slack notifications create an asynchronous review queue.
Both proposals are equivalent because the underlying model capabilities are identical regardless of integration point.

questions.explanation: Proposal A keeps assistance at the point of development, cutting context-switching (C), while Proposal B forces developers out of the IDE and back, adding friction against the productivity objective (B). A trades the objective for auditability, D misreads friction as velocity, E ignores the integration point entirely.

questions.question: You are integrating Claude Code into a team workflow and must complete the design and configuration steps before piloting the integrated workflow. Which two steps must be completed BEFORE piloting the integrated workflow with a small group? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Iterate the integrated workflow based on pilot findings before broader rollout to the team.
Document the integrated workflow with hand-off criteria, permission boundaries, and on-call runbooks.
Negotiate the workflow change with affected teams and obtain formal sign-off from each manager.
Identify the workflow steps where AI-assisted tooling adds value and where human authority must remain.
Configure the project-scope Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, permissions, subagents, and persistent project context.

questions.explanation: Before piloting: identify which workflow steps benefit from AI assistance and where human authority must remain (D), and configure the project-scope MCP servers, permissions, subagents and persistent project context (E). A is post-pilot, B and C follow once the workflow is validated.

questions.question: Engineering leadership wants to roll out Claude Skills to 280 developers across 14 teams. Skills will encode internal coding standards, code review checklists, and incident postmortem templates. Leadership has asked how to govern Skill authorship so that Skills remain trustworthy without bottlenecking on a single central team. Which governance model should you recommend?

options.text: centralized authorship by a single platform team responsible for every Skill produced
fully decentralized authorship across the 14 teams with no review before publication
federated authorship across the 14 teams with a central review and publish gate
per-developer authorship across the 280 engineers with no team-level coordination required

questions.explanation: Federated authorship with a central review and publish gate lets the 14 teams encode their own domain knowledge while keeping a single quality and trust checkpoint. A creates the bottleneck being avoided, B and D remove review entirely.

questions.question: A technical team is debating whether to implement a new capability for generating regulatory filings from internal data as a Claude Skill or as an MCP server. The capability requires a fixed authoring procedure with embedded examples, does not need to call live external systems, and must be portable across three Claude deployments: claude.ai, an internal API integration, and Claude Code. Which factor most strongly favors implementing the capability as a Skill?

options.text: The capability must be callable from a developer's command-line interface as well.
The capability requires authentication against the corporate identity provider directly.
The capability needs to query a live database for the most recent regulatory filings.
The capability is procedural knowledge with no live external system calls required.

questions.explanation: A Skill is the right packaging for procedural knowledge — a fixed authoring procedure with embedded examples — that needs no live system calls and must be portable across claude.ai, an API integration and Claude Code. A, B and C describe live-system and auth needs, which point toward an MCP server.

questions.question: You are defining when to introduce a project subagent versus relying on Claude Code's general capabilities. Which scenario most directly justifies a dedicated subagent?

options.text: The team has a recurring specialized task (such as database schema review) that requires a focused system prompt, narrow tool permissions, and a specific model selection across many sessions.
The team has no recurring specialized tasks and uses Claude Code only for isolated general-purpose work that does not justify a dedicated system prompt or tool scope.
The team wants every Claude Code interaction to use the same generic system prompt with no task-specific specialization, narrow tool permissions, or dedicated model selection.
The team has a one-time ad-hoc question that will not recur and does not require a focused system prompt, narrow tool permissions, or a dedicated model selection.

questions.explanation: A dedicated subagent is justified by a recurring specialised task that benefits from its own focused system prompt, narrow tool permissions and specific model selection across many sessions. B, C and D describe one-off or generic work with no specialisation to encode.

questions.question: You are compiling team-setup practices for a Claude Code rollout across an engineering organization. Which two practices belong on the list? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Use project scope for personal editor preferences so the preferences apply consistently within the project.
Use project scope for team-shared Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and permission rules under version control.
Use local scope for security-critical permission rules so each engineer can adapt them to ongoing work.
Use user scope for team-shared MCP servers so every engineer on the team has consistent access.
Apply managed configuration centrally for security-critical settings that must not be overridden by individual engineers.

questions.explanation: Put team-shared MCP servers and permission rules in project scope under version control (B), and apply managed configuration centrally for security-critical settings that individuals must not override (E). A misplaces personal preferences, C puts security rules where they can be changed locally, D makes shared servers a per-user chore.

questions.question: You are integrating Claude Code into the teams pull-request workflow. The team wants AI-assisted review without removing human approval. Which integration design best fits this requirement?

options.text: Claude Code merges every pull request automatically upon completing its analysis, bypassing the human approval step and the existing branch protection rules entirely.
Claude Code disables all existing branch protection rules on the repository to streamline the merge process, removing human approval as a required gate for all pull requests.
Claude Code silently deletes pull requests it assesses as low quality without posting a comment or notifying the author, removing the author's ability to respond or revise.
Claude Code reviews the pull request and posts a structured analysis as a comment, while a human reviewer retains the approval decision under the existing branch protection rules.

questions.explanation: Claude Code posts a structured review as a PR comment while the human reviewer keeps the approval decision under existing branch protection. A, B and C all remove the human gate.

questions.question: You are identifying inefficiency in a Claude Code workflow where each engineer manually re-explains the project's conventions and architecture in every session. Which adjustment most directly removes this inefficiency?

options.text: Capture the project's conventions and architecture in a project-scoped CLAUDE.md (or equivalent persistent project-context file) committed to the repository, so each session loads it automatically.
Forbid the use of Claude Code on the project entirely to avoid the session-initialization overhead, accepting that the team loses all AI-assisted development productivity for this codebase.
Tell each engineer to retype the project conventions and architecture context more quickly at the start of each session, reducing time lost without eliminating the repeated manual effort.
Remove all documented project conventions and architectural standards so engineers have nothing to re-explain at session start, accepting the loss of consistency and shared coding standards.

questions.explanation: Commit the conventions and architecture to a project-scoped CLAUDE.md (or equivalent persistent project-context file) so every session loads it automatically. B abandons the tool, C only speeds up the waste, D deletes the standards.

questions.question: The compliance team has authored a regulatory disclosure procedure that must be applied identically across customer service, sales, and onboarding workflows. The procedure changes when regulators issue updates, currently four to six times per year. You are designing how the procedure will be packaged for use by Claude across all three workflows. Which two design decisions should you include? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Reference the same Claude Skill from all three of the workflow integrations directly.
Store the procedure in a shared retrieval corpus accessed by all three workflows.
Have each workflow team rewrite the procedure for that team's specific context.
Package the procedure as a Claude Skill owned by the compliance team directly.
Embed the procedure text into each workflow's system prompt at integration time.

questions.explanation: Package the procedure once as a Skill owned by the compliance team (D) and reference that same Skill from all three workflow integrations (A), so the four-to-six annual regulatory updates are made in one place. B loses the fixed procedural form, C forks the procedure three ways, E requires three redeployments per update.

questions.question: You are supporting an engineer whose Claude Code session reports a permission denial when the engineer expected the action to be allowed. Which resolution step is most appropriate?

options.text: Disable the permission system entirely across all scopes to remove the denial, eliminating all tool-pattern and deny-rule controls rather than identifying and amending the specific rule.
Grant the engineer unrestricted Bash access to bypass the specific rule causing the denial, removing all tool-pattern constraints rather than amending only the rule in question.
Tell the engineer to retry the denied action verbatim repeatedly until the denial stops appearing, without inspecting the active permission rules to determine whether the denial is intentional.

Inspect the active permission rules across all scopes (managed, command-line, local, project, user) to identify which rule is denying the action and confirm whether it should be amended or whether the action should remain denied.

questions.explanation: Inspect the active permission rules across all scopes (managed, command-line, local, project, user) to find which rule denies the action and decide whether it should be amended or is correctly denying. A, B and C remove controls or ignore the cause.

questions.question: You are resolving a Claude Code operational issue reported by the team and must complete the diagnostic steps before applying a targeted fix. Which two steps must be completed BEFORE applying the targeted fix? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Open a permanent change request in the change-management system to formalize the upcoming fix.
Document the root cause and the fix in the team runbook for future occurrences.
Form a hypothesis about the most likely root cause given the symptom, configuration, and recent changes.
Reproduce the issue with a minimal reproduction case to confirm the symptom and isolate variables.
Notify the affected users that a fix has been deployed and the operational issue is resolved.

questions.explanation: Diagnosis before fix: reproduce the issue with a minimal case to confirm the symptom and isolate variables (D), and form a hypothesis about the root cause given symptom, configuration and recent changes (C). A, B and E surround or follow the fix.

questions.question: A Claude architect is configuring a shared Claude Code environment for a twelve-person development team. Which two configuration decisions most directly establish a consistent, secure team environment? (Choose two.)

options.text: applying managed configuration to enforce non-overridable security and compliance policies across all team members
committing shared MCP server definitions and tool permissions in project-scope configuration files alongside the repository
instructing each engineer to configure their preferred Claude model in personal user-scope settings
storing the team's shared API key in the project-scope settings.json so all engineers use the same credential
setting editor theme and display preferences at the project scope so they are uniform across workstations

questions.explanation: Managed configuration enforces non-overridable security and compliance policy across the team (A), and project-scope files committed alongside the repo give everyone the same MCP servers and tool permissions (B). C is a personal preference, D commits a shared credential to the repo, E puts display settings in the wrong scope.

questions.question: You are configuring Claude Code for a team that needs every engineer to share the same MCP server set, permission rules, and project context across the engineering monorepo. Which configuration scope best supports this requirement?

options.text: user scope configured individually on each engineer's machine, with no shared configuration committed to the repository and no guarantee of consistency across the team
user scope with the MCP server definitions and permission rules placed in each engineer's ~/.claude/settings.json and synchronized manually via a shared setup script outside version control
local scope configured only on the lead architect's machine, with no configuration present on other engineers' machines and no mechanism to distribute MCP servers or permission rules
project scope, with the configuration committed to the repository so every engineer working in the project picks up the same MCP servers, permissions, and context

questions.explanation: Project scope committed to the repository gives every engineer the same MCP servers, permission rules and project context automatically. A, B and C all depend on per-machine setup with no guarantee of consistency.

questions.question: A Claude needs to ensure that a security-hardening flag cannot be disabled by any individual engineer after it is set. Which configuration scope correctly enforces this requirement?

options.text: managed configuration applied centrally and marked as non-overridable
environment variable defined in the CI/CD pipeline only
project scope (.claude/settings.json) committed to the repository
user scope (~/.claude/settings.json) on each engineer's machine

questions.explanation: Managed configuration applied centrally and marked non-overridable is the only scope an individual engineer cannot change. Project and user scope are editable locally, and a CI-only environment variable does not govern engineers' sessions.

questions.question: You are integrating Claude Code into a workflow that runs against a production database. Which guardrail design most directly preserves safety on data-modifying operations?

options.text: Allow Claude Code to write directly to the production database without subagent scoping, read-only credential defaults, or human confirmation gates on data-modifying operations.
Configure the database MCP server with a fully privileged credential that can perform any read or write operation, and allow all operations to proceed without explicit human confirmation.

Configure the database MCP server with a read-only credential by default, restrict the subagent's tool list to read-only operations, and require explicit human confirmation on any operation that would modify data.
Disable all logging and auditing on database operations through the MCP server to reduce alert noise, removing the observability needed to detect unintended data modifications.

questions.explanation: Defence in depth on writes: a read-only credential by default on the database MCP server, a subagent tool list restricted to read operations, and explicit human confirmation on any data-modifying operation. A and B grant unchecked write access, D removes the audit trail.

questions.question: A Claude architect is auditing configuration scope assignments. Which two statements correctly identify an appropriate use of user-scope configuration versus other scopes? (Choose two.)

options.text: defining MCP server endpoints shared by all contributors to a specific repository
persisting personal editor theme preferences that follow an engineer across projects
saving a preferred Claude response language that applies to all repositories the engineer uses
storing API authentication keys so they are not committed to version control
enforcing a company-wide policy that disables a feature for all engineers

questions.explanation: User scope carries personal settings that follow the engineer across projects: editor theme preferences (B) and a preferred response language for all repositories (C). A belongs in project scope, D belongs in a secret store or environment, E belongs in managed configuration.

questions.question: You are rolling out a standardized Claude Code configuration to an engineering team and must complete the planning steps before piloting the configuration. Which two steps must be completed BEFORE piloting the configuration with a small group of engineers? (Choose two.) Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Roll out the stabilized configuration to additional teams with documentation and a defined support channel.
Define the project-scope baseline covering Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, permission rules, and subagents.
Onboard every engineer in the organization to the new configuration through mandatory training sessions.
Iterate the configuration based on the pilot findings and stabilize the baseline before broader rollout.
Identify the team workflows, security boundaries, and which decisions belong to managed configuration versus project scope.

questions.explanation: Before piloting: identify team workflows, security boundaries and which decisions belong to managed configuration versus project scope (E), then define the project-scope baseline of MCP servers, permission rules and subagents (B). A, C and D come after the pilot.

questions.question: You are supporting a team whose Claude Code sessions consistently load 60 or more MCP tools from many servers, exhausting context budget before the session begins. Which adjustment most directly addresses this issue without removing capability?

options.text: Enable Tool Search so tool definitions are deferred and discovered on demand rather than loaded into context upfront.
Add additional MCP servers to give the team more capability, which increases rather than reduces the number of tool definitions loaded into the session's context budget.
Increase the prompt's verbosity with additional instructions and context, which consumes more of the context budget rather than reducing the tool-definition overhead causing the issue.
Disable every MCP server in the configuration to free up context budget, accepting that the team loses all tool access and cannot perform any MCP-dependent task in the session.

questions.explanation: Tool Search defers tool definitions and discovers them on demand, so 60+ tools no longer consume context before the session starts, and no capability is removed. B worsens the problem, C is unrelated, D removes capability.

questions.question: A team manager wants all engineers working on the same repository to share identical MCP server definitions without manual synchronization. Which configuration approach satisfies this requirement?

options.text: project-scope .claude/settings.json and .mcp.json files committed to the repository
managed configuration pushed to all endpoints by the administrator
environment variables set at the operating-system level on each workstation
each engineer maintains a personal ~/.claude/settings.json with the shared definitions

questions.explanation: Project-scope .claude/settings.json and .mcp.json committed to the repository distribute identical MCP server definitions to everyone working in it, with no manual sync. B is for centrally enforced policy, C and D require per-machine maintenance.

questions.question: You are diagnosing a Claude Code session whose subagent uses 50,000 tokens of context before the engineer types a single message. Which root cause is most likely?

options.text: Many MCP servers are configured, each contributing tool definitions to the context budget; Tool Search is not enabled, so all definitions load upfront.
The model has internal personal preferences or default behaviors that silently consume large portions of context budget before any user message is processed, independent of tool configuration.
The developer's keyboard layout or input-method configuration is the cause of the elevated context consumption, introducing extra tokens before the engineer types any message.
The font rendering or display-scaling settings of the IDE are converting visual output into additional context tokens, causing the high pre session context consumption.

questions.explanation: Many configured MCP servers each contribute tool definitions to the context budget, and without Tool Search enabled every definition is loaded upfront. B, C and D are not mechanisms that consume context tokens.

questions.question: You are explaining the precedence of Claude Code configuration scopes to the team. Which precedence ordering, from highest to lowest, is correct?

options.text: Local --> managed --> user --> command-line arguments --> project
Managed --> command-line arguments --> local --> project --> user
User --> project --> local --> command-line arguments --> managed
Project --> user --> managed --> local --> project command-line arguments

questions.explanation: Highest to lowest: managed (enterprise) settings, then command-line arguments, then local project settings, then shared project settings, then user settings. The other orderings invert the managed-at-top and user-at-bottom rule.

questions.question: You are reviewing a peer's Claude Code permission rules for an enterprise rollout. The rules grant unrestricted Bash access to all projects across all developers. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Approve the unrestricted Bash access as written on the grounds that narrowing the rules would add configuration complexity, accepting the full attack surface for all engineers across all projects.
Replace unrestricted Bash with narrowly-scoped tool patterns that allow only the specific commands the workflows require, and add explicit deny rules for sensitive operations.
Add unrestricted access to additional tool categories as well, so that Bash is not asymmetrically more permissive than other tools, expanding the attack surface further in the name of consistency.
Disable all permission rules for the enterprise rollout so every command across every project runs without any tool-pattern scoping or explicit deny rules for sensitive operations.

questions.explanation: Replace unrestricted Bash with narrowly scoped tool patterns covering only the commands the workflows need, plus explicit deny rules for sensitive operations. A accepts the full attack surface, C and D widen it.

questions.question: You are integrating AI-assisted tooling into the teams documentation workflow. The team wants generated documentation that stays grounded in the actual code. Which integration approach best fits this requirement?

options.text: Disable all filesystem and code-search tools so the subagents cannot read any repository code, accepting that documentation generation will be entirely disconnected from the actual implementation.
Generate documentation from the model's training-data recall without reading any of the actual repository code, accepting that the output will not reflect the current implementation.
Configure subagents that read the relevant code files via filesystem and code-search tools, generate the documentation, and emit changes through the teams normal review workflow.
Have the subagents publish generated documentation directly to the public-facing site without passing through the team's normal review workflow or any human approval step.

questions.explanation: Ground the documentation in the repository itself: subagents read the relevant code through filesystem and code-search tools, generate the docs, and route the changes through the team's normal review workflow. A and B disconnect output from the code, D bypasses review.

questions.question: You are supporting an engineer whose newly added MCP server does not appear in their Claude Code session. Which diagnostic step should be tried first?

options.text: Reinstall the developer's operating system from scratch, discarding all local configuration and tool state before attempting any targeted diagnostic steps.
Disable every MCP server in the configuration to isolate the issue, removing all tool access rather than confirming whether the new server is registered.
Switch the team to a different Claude product family unrelated to the existing workflow, abandoning the current configuration rather than diagnosing the registration issue.
Verify the MCP server is registered using the listing command, then reconnect the session if needed, since configuration changes typically require a restart to take effect.

questions.explanation: Start with the cheapest check that confirms registration: list the configured MCP servers, then reconnect or restart the session, since configuration changes generally require a restart to take effect. A, B and C are disproportionate before basic verification.

questions.question: You are comparing two configurations for an internal compliance Q&A assistant. Configuration X reduces top-k retrieval and uses a lighter model, lowering p95 latency by 38 percent while producing a measured 2 percent reduction in the accuracy benchmark. Configuration Y retains the existing top-k retrieval setting and heavier model, with unchanged p95 latency and no measurable change in accuracy. The deployment's stated priorities are accuracy first and latency second. Which configuration is the better recommendation?

options.text: Configuration X, because the 2 percent accuracy reduction falls within normal benchmark variance and is not a meaningful regression.
Configuration Y, because the deployment's stated priority is accuracy first, and Configuration X produces a measured reduction in accuracy.
Configuration X, because lower latency generally matters more than accuracy, regardless of the deployment's stated priorities.
Configuration X, because a 38 percent latency improvement outweighs a 2 percent accuracy reduction as a general rule across compliance deployments.

questions.explanation: The deployment's stated priorities are accuracy first and latency second, and Configuration X produces a measured accuracy loss, so Y is the right recommendation (B). A dismisses a measured regression as noise without evidence; C and D apply a generic rule that ignores the stated priorities.

questions.question: A software vendor wants to build a RAG assistant over its own internal support-ticket archive (not the public web) and needs the same quality of source attribution that citation-grounded answers provide, without sending queries to an external search index. Which feature fits this requirement?

options.text: Search results, because it provides citation-quality source attribution for custom knowledge bases outside the public web.
Code execution, because running retrieval scripts in a sandbox lets the model fetch and cite ticket content directly.
Web fetch, because retrieving full page content from specified URLs works equally well for private ticket archives.
Web search tool, because it augments Claude's knowledge with current information regardless of where the documents are hosted.

questions.explanation: Search result content blocks let your own retrieval system return passages with source and title metadata, so Claude cites them with the same quality as web-search citations, without any external index (A). Code execution (B) is not an attribution mechanism; web fetch (C) and the web search tool (D) target public URLs and the web.

questions.domain: Claude Models, Prompting and Context Engineering
questions.question: A long-running autonomous coding agent needs two things in its architecture: automatically clearing stale tool results from context as a session approaches the token limit, and retaining key project facts across separate sessions run days apart. Select all components that correctly satisfy these two needs.

options.text: Compaction, positioned as the sole mechanism that fully replaces context editing for long-running sessions
Code execution, which runs code in a sandboxed container for data analysis and file processing tasks
The memory tool, which lets Claude store and retrieve information across separate conversations over time
Fine-grained tool streaming, which reduces latency by streaming tool parameters without JSON buffering
The Files API, which lets uploaded documents be referenced repeatedly without re-uploading their content
Context editing, which supports clearing tool results automatically as a conversation approaches the token limit

questions.explanation: Context editing clears stale tool results automatically as the conversation approaches the token limit (F), and the memory tool stores and retrieves facts across separate conversations (C). A is wrong because compaction does not fully replace context editing; code execution, fine-grained tool streaming and the Files API address neither need.

questions.question: A team is choosing between orchestrator-workers and parallelization by sectioning for a document-analysis pipeline. Which statements correctly distinguish orchestrator-workers from parallelization by sectioning?

options.text: Orchestrator-workers and parallelization by sectioning both aggregate multiple independent votes on one input to reach a majority-based answer
Orchestrator-workers suits subtasks that vary unpredictably case to case, while sectioning suits tasks that split cleanly into known subtasks
Parallelization by sectioning always requires a second LLM to evaluate the sectioned outputs before combining them into a final result
In orchestrator-workers, worker LLMs run in a fixed, predetermined order, whereas sectioning always runs its subtasks simultaneously
In orchestrator-workers, a central LLM determines subtasks at runtime, whereas sectioning requires subtasks predefined before execution

questions.explanation: In orchestrator-workers a central LLM decides the subtasks at runtime, which suits work that varies unpredictably; sectioning splits a task into subtasks known before execution (B, E). A describes the voting variant of parallelization; C invents a mandatory evaluator; D is wrong because workers are not run in a fixed order.

questions.question: A team is building an agent that must audit a large codebase across three distinct dimensions: security vulnerabilities, code quality, and test coverage. Each dimension requires a different set of tools and a different area of focus. Which approach best decomposes this problem using the Agent SDK?

options.text: Define an orchestrator agent that invokes specialized subagents through the Agent tool, each configured with a scoped tool set and description matching its subtask domain
Send one prompt to the main agent instructing it to sequentially perform code quality checks, then security scanning, then test coverage analysis without additional configuration
Increase the primary agent's context window and rely on extended thinking so it can reason through all three review dimensions within one continuous session
Configure a single MCP server that exposes security, quality, and coverage checks as three separate tools, and let the primary agent call each tool directly instead of delegating

questions.explanation: Three independent dimensions, each with its own tools and focus, map naturally to an orchestrator that delegates to specialized subagents with scoped tool sets and descriptions (A). B keeps everything in one undifferentiated prompt, C relies on a bigger context instead of decomposition, and D still leaves one agent juggling all three concerns.

questions.question: An enterprise customer's support desk has committed to a contractual 99.9% uptime and sub-2-second p95 response SLA for its Claude-powered ticket triage assistant. During architecture review, the team must select which platform capabilities to prioritize primarily to protect this SLA commitment. Which two capabilities are the most directly relevant to protecting a latency and availability SLA? (Select 2)

options.text: Server-side fallback, which retries a refused request against a backup model within the same API call for a timely response
Choosing a model with faster comparative latency, such as Claude Haiku 4.5, for the latency-sensitive triage path
The Files API, which lets documents be uploaded once and referenced across multiple requests without re-uploading content
Batch processing, which processes large volumes of requests asynchronously at a discounted rate over an extended completion window
Agent Skills, which extend Claude's capabilities with pre-built instructions and scripts for document-format tasks

questions.explanation: An SLA of this kind covers availability and latency: server-side fallback keeps requests answered when the primary model refuses or fails (A), and a faster model such as Haiku 4.5 protects the p95 latency target (B). Batch processing is asynchronous and slow; the Files API and Agent Skills do not bear on the SLA.

questions.domain: Claude Models, Prompting and Context Engineering
questions.question: A manufacturing client wants a Claude-based quality-inspection assistant that repeatedly analyzes the same reference specification documents alongside new inspection reports throughout the day. The client's stated goal is to reduce redundant token spend on the unchanging reference material while keeping individual inspection turnaround fast. Which architectural choice best serves this efficiency and cost goal?

options.text: Use prompt caching so the unchanging reference specification is cached and reused across requests, cutting cost and latency
Increase the effort parameter to xhigh on every inspection request so Claude reasons more thoroughly each time
Re-upload the full reference specification as plain text in every single request to guarantee the model always has the latest version
Move the entire workload to the Message Batches API so all inspection reports are processed together once per day

questions.explanation: The reference specification is identical across many requests, which is exactly what prompt caching is for: the cached prefix is reused, lowering cost and latency (A). Higher effort (B) increases spend, re-sending the full text (C) is the redundancy to remove, and once-a-day batching (D) breaks the fast-turnaround requirement.

questions.question: A coding assistant must modify an unknown number of files across a repository to implement a feature, where the exact files and scope of changes can only be determined once the assistant inspects the codebase. Which pattern is most appropriate?

options.text: Routing, where the assistant classifies the feature request and sends it to one of several fixed file-editing prompts
Parallelization by sectioning, where the assistant edits every file in the repository simultaneously using a predetermined split
Prompt chaining, where the assistant edits files in a fixed sequence determined before inspecting the repository
Orchestrator-workers, where a central LLM inspects the repository and dynamically delegates each file edit to a worker LLM

questions.explanation: The number of files and the scope of changes are only known after inspecting the codebase, so subtasks must be decided at runtime by a central LLM that delegates to workers (D). Routing (A), predetermined sectioning (B) and fixed prompt chaining (C) all require the steps to be known in advance.

questions.question: A developer is building an email-triage agent that reads inbound email bodies via a tool and drafts replies. To harden it against embedded instructions in email bodies, which combination of design choices should the developer apply? (Select all that apply)

options.text: State a system prompt policy that content returned by tools is untrusted data and must never override the system prompt or the user's original request
Place the developer's own operating instructions inside the same tool_result block as the email body so both travel together in one message
JSON-encode the email body when passing it as a tool result so quotes or tags in the content cannot break out of the surrounding structure
Screen tool outputs with a lightweight classifier model before passing them to the main agent, and strip or flag content if an injection is suspected
Grant the agent broad, unscoped access to the user's full mailbox and account settings so it never needs to ask for additional permissions mid-task

questions.explanation: Defending against indirect prompt injection means treating tool output as untrusted data in the system prompt (A), encoding it so content cannot break out of its structure (C), and screening it with a classifier before the main agent sees it (D). Mixing your own instructions into the tool_result (B) blurs data and instructions, and broad unscoped access (E) magnifies the damage of a successful injection.

questions.domain: Claude Models, Prompting and Context Engineering
questions.question: A team is building an English-to-Spanish translation feature that will be called repeatedly with different user-submitted text. They want to keep the instructional wording consistent across calls while making it easy to swap in new text and track changes to the instructions separately from the text being translated. Which approach best fits this goal?

options.text: Define a prompt template with the fixed instruction text and a placeholder such as {{text}}, substituting only the variable content on each call while the surrounding instructions stay constant.

Send the fixed instruction text and the user's text to the model in two separate API calls, then concatenate the responses, placing the translation after the instruction output to form the final result.

Regenerate the complete translation prompt on every call by constructing the instruction string dynamically with the user's text, ensuring that each request carries an up-to-date version of the wording.
Store the entire prompt containing the fixed instructions and the user's text as one static string, editing the string by hand for each new translation request so the prompt is always up to date.

questions.explanation: A prompt template keeps the fixed instructions constant and substitutes only the variable text through a placeholder such as {{text}}, so the instructions can be versioned separately (A). Splitting into two calls (B) breaks the task, rebuilding the prompt each call (C) loses the stable wording, and hand-editing one static string (D) mixes instructions and data.

questions.domain: Claude Models, Prompting and Context Engineering
questions.question: An agent runs long tool-use loops involving dozens of file reads per session. The team wants old tool results automatically cleared once input tokens exceed 30,000, while always preserving the 3 most recent tool exchanges and never clearing results from the web_search tool. Which context_management configuration achieves this?

options.text: A clear_tool_uses_20250919 edit with trigger set to tool_uses 30000, with no keep value explicitly set, and with no exclude_tools value explicitly set.
A clear_thinking_20251015 edit with trigger set to 30000 input tokens, keep set to 3 thinking turns, and exclude_tools set to web_search should be used.
A clear_tool_uses_20250919 edit with trigger set to 30000 input tokens, keep set to 3 tool uses, and exclude_tools set to file_read should be used.
Configure a clear_tool_uses_20250919 edit with trigger set to 30000 input tokens, keep 3 tool uses, exclude_tools set to web_search.

questions.explanation: All three conditions must match: a clear_tool_uses_20250919 edit triggered at 30,000 input tokens, keeping the 3 most recent tool uses, and excluding web_search from clearing (D). A triggers on the wrong unit and sets no keep or exclusion, B uses the thinking-clearing edit, and C excludes the wrong tool.

questions.domain: Claude Models, Prompting and Context Engineering
questions.question: A code-review prompt needs Claude to generate a fix, verify the fix against a set of criteria, and then refine the fix if criteria are not met. The team wants to inspect the intermediate review step and log it separately before the final refinement is produced. Which approach best fits this requirement?

options.text: Break the task into separate API calls: generate a fix, review it against the criteria, then refine the fix, so each step can be logged independently.
Ask Claude to generate, verify, and refine the fix in one response using extended reasoning, but this keeps the review internal and unloggable.
Add tags around the review step so Claude places the review inside and the fix outside, and the review can be extracted and logged apart.
Provide five few-shot examples of correct fixes for Claude to mimic, bypassing the review step, removing the intermediate step and preventing logging.

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining splits generate, review and refine into separate API calls, so the intermediate review is a distinct output that can be inspected and logged before refinement (A). A single response (B) hides the review, tags (C) still produce one combined output in one call, and few-shot examples (D) remove the review step altogether.

questions.question: A platform wants Claude to discover tools using an existing embeddings index rather than the built-in regex or BM25 matching, because tool descriptions are sparse but semantically related through the embedding space. Which implementation matches this requirement?

options.text: Build a custom tool that runs the embeddings search and returns tool_reference blocks in its tool_result for Claude to expand.
Enable the built-in regex tool search variant and rely on broad wildcard patterns to approximate semantic matching.
Disable tool search and load every tool definition up front so the embeddings index becomes unnecessary.
Enable the built-in BM25 tool search variant, since BM25 ranking approximates embedding-based semantic similarity closely enough.

questions.explanation: When the built-in regex and BM25 variants are not a fit, you can implement your own tool search: a custom tool runs the embeddings query and returns tool_reference blocks in its tool_result for Claude to expand (A). Wildcard regex (B) and BM25 (D) remain lexical matching, and loading every tool up front (C) gives up tool search instead of improving it.

questions.question: A support-ticket assistant retrieves passages from a 500-document internal knowledge base for each incoming ticket and must cite the exact source passage in every reply, without re-sending the entire corpus on each request. Which approach best matches this data shape and query pattern?

options.text: Upload all 500 documents as citable text documents in the system prompt so that Claude can reference any passage directly, and then instruct it to cite the source document and section for every reply.

Store the corpus in the memory tool by saving each document as a separate entry, configure assistant to load all entries before answering, and prompt it to cite source document for any retrieved passage.
Return the retrieved passages as search result content blocks from a retrieval tool, each carrying source and title metadata, so Claude generates natural citations per ticket.
